{{Short description|Higher-order frequency analysis}}

'''Polyspectra''', also known as '''higher-order spectra''', are frequency-domain statistical quantities that generalize the  [[spectral density]] (power spectrum) to higher orders. Polyspectra of a given signal can reveal non-[[Gaussian process|Gaussian]] behavior, time-inversion asymmetries, and phase correlations between different frequency contributions to the signal. While a standard power spectrum quantifies the distribution of intensity across frequencies, polyspectra characterize higher-order phase and amplitude correlations between frequency components. Higher-order spectra include the third-order [[bispectrum]], the fourth-order trispectrum, and their multivariate generalizations.

== Definition ==

In his original publications, Brillinger considers a [[stationary process]] (the signal) <math>z(t)</math> and its multi-time [[cumulant]].<ref name="Brillinger1965">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Brillinger
 | first1 = David R.
 | title = An introduction to polyspectra
 | journal = The Annals of Mathematical Statistics
 | volume = 36
 | issue = 5
 | pages = 1351–1374
 | year = 1965
 | doi = 10.1214/aoms/1177699896
 | url = https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-mathematical-statistics/volume-36/issue-5/An-Introduction-to-Polyspectra/10.1214/aoms/1177699896.full
| doi-access = free
 }}</ref>  
<math display = "block">
f(\tau_1,\cdots ,\tau_{n-1}) = C_n(z(t),z(t+\tau_1),\cdots,z(t+\tau_{n-1})).
</math>
The cumulant does not depend on <math>t</math> since <math>z(t)</math> is stationary. This allows for a definition of <math>n</math>-th order 
polyspectra  <math>S^{(n)}_z</math> of a stationary signal <math>z(t)</math> by
<math display="block">
C_n\big(z(\omega_1),\cdots,z(\omega_n)\big) = 2 \pi \delta(\omega_1 + \cdots + \omega_n) S^{(n)}_z(\omega_1,\cdots,\omega_{n-1})
</math>
with the [[Fourier transform]]
<math>
  z(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{i\omega \tau} z(\tau)  d\tau,
</math>
and the [[Dirac delta function]] <math>\delta</math> which appears due to the independence 
of <math>f</math> on <math>t</math>.
<ref name="Ubbelohde2012">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Ubbelohde
 | first1 = Niels
 | last2 = Fricke
 | first2 = Christian
 | last3 = Flindt
 | first3 = Christian
 | last4 = Hohls
 | first4 = Frank
 | last5 = Haug
 | first5 = Rolf J.
 | title = Measurement of finite‑frequency current statistics in a single‑electron transistor
 | journal = Nature Communications
 | volume = 3
 | page = 612
 | year = 2012
 | doi = 10.1038/ncomms1620
  | doi-access = free| url = https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms1620
| arxiv = 1201.2163
 }}</ref>

The second order spectrum can be rewritten as 
<math display="block">
S_z^{(2)} (\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{i\omega \tau} C_2(z(t+\tau),z(t)) d\tau,
</math>
where <math> C_2(x, y) = \langle xy \rangle - \langle x \rangle \langle y \rangle </math> is the [[covariance]]. 
The representation of <math>S_z^{(2)}</math> is equivalent to the definition of the
[[spectral density]] of <math>z</math> (power spectrum) as Fourier transform of the [[autocorrelation function]] of <math>z(t)</math>.

== History of polyspectra ==
Higher-order spectra were formalized in the works of Brillinger starting in the 1950s.<ref name="Brillinger1965" /> Mendel and Nikias contributed the first major reviews on the topic in the early 1990s,<ref name="Mendel1991">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Mendel
 | first1 = Jerry M.
 | title = Tutorial on higher‑order statistics (spectra) in signal processing and system theory: theoretical results and some applications
 | journal = Proceedings of the IEEE
 | volume = 79
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 278–305
 | year = 1991
 | doi = 10.1109/5.75086
 | url = https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/75086
| url-access = subscription
 }}</ref><ref name="Nikias1993">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Nikias
 | first1 = C. L.
 | title = Signal processing with higher‑order spectra
 | journal = IEEE Signal Processing Magazine
 | volume = 10
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 10–37
 | year = 1993
 | doi = 10.1109/79.221324
 | url = https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/221324| url-access = subscription
 }}</ref> resulting in the "Higher Order Spectral Analysis Toolbox" (HOSA), a software library that included the bispectrum and some fourth order statistics.<ref>{{cite book
| last1 = Swami
| first1 = Ananthram
| last2 = Mendel
| first2 = Jerry M.
| last3 = Nikias
| first3 = Chrysostomos L.
| title = Higher-Order Spectral Analysis Toolbox: User's Guide
| year = 1993
| publisher = United Signals & Systems, Inc.
| location = Compton, CA
| url = https://www.ai.rug.nl/~signaal/help/signal_tb.pdf
}}</ref>
However, Birkelund stated in 2003: "In theory, polyspectra can be applied to solve many important problems in signal processing and data analysis. In practice, however, one has been discouraged by the poor statistical properties of most polyspectral estimators."<ref name="birkelund2003">{{cite journal
| last1 = Birkelund
| first1 = Yngve
| last2 = Hanssen
| first2 = Alfred
| last3 = Powers
| first3 = Edward J.
| title = Multitaper estimators of polyspectra
| journal = Signal Processing
| volume = 83
| issue = 3
| pages = 545–559
| year = 2003
| doi = 10.1016/S0165-1684(02)00484-X
}}</ref> In 2026, unbiased cumulant-based estimators for higher-order spectra were proposed and analyzed.<ref name="Sifft2026" /> They are implemented in GPU-accelerated software libraries based on ArrayFire<ref>{{cite web
 | title = SignalSnap: Spectra at your fingertips
 | url = https://github.com/MarkusSifft/SignalSnap/
 | website = GitHub
 | publisher = MarkusSifft
 | access-date = 26 February 2026
 | quote = SignalSnap is an open-source Python toolbox for higher-order spectral analysis of time series that efficiently calculates power spectra, bispectra, and trispectra and supports hardware-accelerated computation.
}}</ref> and alternatively based on PyTorch.<ref>{{cite web
 | title = SignalSnap-PyTorch: SignalSnap rewritten in PyTorch, added multi-channel options and optimized
 | url = https://github.com/ArminGEtemad/SignalSnap-PyTorch/
 | website = GitHub
 | publisher = ArminGEtemad
 | access-date = 26 February 2026
 | quote = SignalSnap rewritten in PyTorch, with multi-channel options and optimization; this version transitions the backend from ArrayFire to PyTorch for enhanced usability and performance.
}}</ref>

== Numerics of polyspectra ==
The definition of polyspectra assumes a [[stationary process]] <math>z(t)</math> that is known with an infinite temporal resolution in an infinite temporal interval. Real world data <math>z(t)</math> allow therefore only for the calculation of estimates of polyspectra. These estimates have finite spectral resolution and finite accuracy.

=== Classical estimators ===
Direct Fourier methods usually start with the Fourier transform of the entire signal resulting in a high frequency resolution with large variance (error). Subsequently, a smoothing kernel can be applied to trade resolution for variance. Alternatively, spectra of segments of the signal are averaged (Welch-type method).
<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1=Hinich
 | first1=Melvin J.
 | last2=Clay
 | first2=Christian S.
 | title= The application of the discrete Fourier transform in the estimation of power spectra, coherence, and bispectra of geophysical data
 | journal=Reviews of Geophysics
 | volume=6
 | issue=3
 | pages = 347–363
 | year=1968
 | doi = 10.1029/RG006i003p00347
}}</ref>

The lag window method relies on estimating cumulants in the time-domain and subsequent application of Fourier transforms.

Multitaper methods consider the entire signal tapered (windowed) with orthogonal tapers. Spectra for separate tapers are then averaged.<ref name="birkelund2003"/>

The classical methods rely on cumulant estimators that are only asymptotically unbiased.

=== Unbiased cumulant-based estimators ===
The following equations provide an unbiased estimate ([[estimator]]) of polyspectra up to fourth order.<ref name = "Sifft2026">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Sifft
 | first1 = Markus
 | last2 = Ghorbanietemad
 | first2 = Armin
 | last3 = Wagner
 | first3 = Fabian
 | last4 = Hägele
 | first4 = Daniel
 | title = Correct estimation of higher-order spectra: From theoretical challenges to practical multi-channel implementation in SignalSnap
 | journal = Digital Signal Processing
 | volume = 173
 | year = 2026
 | article-number = 105893
 | doi = 10.1016/j.dsp.2026.105893
 | url = https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1051200426000138
| doi-access = free
 }}</ref>
Fourier coefficients of <math>z(t)</math> 
<math display="block">
a_k = \frac{T}{N} \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} g_j z_j e^{2 \pi i k j/ N}\,,
</math>
are calculated from the process
<math>z_j = z(jT/N - t_0)</math> which is divided into windows of length <math>T</math> with <math>N</math> points per window. A [[window function]] <math>g_j = g(jT/N)</math> reduces spectral leakage.

Approximate polyspectra are obtained from cumulants of Fourier coefficients:
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
&\text{Average: }&S_z^{(1)} &\approx \frac{N C_1(a_0)}{T \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} g_j}\\
\\[2pt]
&\text{Power spectrum: }&S_z^{(2)}(\omega_k) &\approx \frac{N C_2(a_k, a_k^*)}{T \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} g_j g_j^*}\\
\\[2pt]
&\text{Bispectrum: }&S_z^{(3)}(\omega_k, \omega_l) &\approx \frac{N C_3(a_k, a_l, a_{k+l}^*)}{T \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} g_j^2 g_j^*}\\
\\[2pt]
&\text{Trispectrum: }&S_z^{(4)}(\omega_k, \omega_l, \omega_p) &\approx \frac{N C_4(a_k, a_l, a_p, a_{k+l+p}^*)}{T \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} g_j^3 g_j^*}.\\
\end{align}
</math>
The distances of the spectral positions <math>\omega_k = 2 \pi k / T</math> decrease with increasing window length <math>T</math> resulting in a higher spectral resolution. 
The cumulants <math>C_n</math> can be estimated by the [[k-statistic]] which provides unbiased estimators <math>c_n</math>  ([[estimator]]).<ref name="Fisher1928">{{cite journal 
| last = Fisher 
| first = Ronald A. 
| author-link = Ronald Fisher 
| year = 1928 
| title = Moments and Product Moments of Sampling Distributions 
| journal = [[Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society]] 
| series = Second Series 
| volume = 30 
| issue = 1 
| pages = 199–238 
| doi = 10.1112/plms/s2-30.1.199 
}}</ref>
<ref name="Kendall1943">{{cite book 
| last = Kendall 
| first = Maurice G. 
| year = 1943 
| title = The Advanced Theory of Statistics 
| edition = 1st 
| volume = 1 
| location = London 
| publisher = Charles Griffin & Company
| url = https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.57860
}}</ref>
<ref name="Cook1951">{{cite journal 
| last = Cook 
| first = M. B. 
| year = 1951 
| title = Bi-variate k-statistics and cumulants of their joint sampling distribution 
| journal = [[Biometrika]] 
| volume = 38 
| issue = 1/2 
| pages = 179–195 
| doi = 10.1093/biomet/38.1-2.179 
}}</ref>
The estimators are given by<ref name="Schefczik2019">{{cite arxiv
 | last1 = Schefczik
 | first1 = Fabian
 | last2 = Hägele
 | first2 = Daniel
 | year = 2019
 | eprint = 1904.12154
 | class=math.ST
 | title = Ready‑to‑Use Unbiased Estimators for Multivariate Cumulants Including One That Outperforms <math>x^3</math>}}</ref>
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
&c_2(x,y) = \frac{m}{m - 1} (\overline{xy} - \overline{x}\,\overline{y})\\
\\[2pt]
&c_3(x, y, z) = \frac{m^2}{(m - 1) (m - 2)} (\overline{xyz} - \overline{xy}\,\overline{z} - \overline{xz}\,\overline{y} - \overline{yz}\,\overline{x} + 2 \overline{x}\,\overline{y}\,\overline{z})\\
\\[2pt]
&c_4(x, y, z, w) = \frac{m^2}{(m - 1) (m - 2) (m - 3)} \big[(m + 1)\overline{xyzw}\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad - (m + 1)(\overline{xyz}\,\overline{w} + \overline{xyw}\,\overline{z} + \overline{xzw}\,\overline{y} + \overline{yzw}\,\overline{x}) \\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad - (m - 1) (\overline{xy}\,\overline{zw} + \overline{xz}\,\,\overline{yw} + \overline{xw}\,\overline{yz}) \\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad + 2m(\overline{xy}\,\overline{z}\,\overline{w} + \overline{xz}\,\overline{y}\,\overline{w} + \overline{xw}\,\overline{y}\,\overline{z} + \overline{yz}\,\overline{x}\,\overline{w} + \overline{yw}\,\overline{x}\,\overline{z} + \overline{zw}\,\overline{x}\,\overline{y})\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad - 6m\overline{x}\,\overline{y}\,\overline{z}\,\overline{w}
\big],
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>\overline{(..)}</math> denotes the average of <math>m</math> samples.

== Applications ==
Bispectra find medical applications in the analysis of  electroencephalograms
<ref name="Sigl1994">{{cite journal |last1=Sigl |first1=J. C. |last2=Champlin |first2=N. P. |title=Bispectral analysis of the electroencephalogram: a review |journal=Journal of Clinical Monitoring |date=1994 |volume=10 |issue=6 |pages=392–404 |doi=10.1007/BF01618421 |pmid=7836975}}</ref>
and are used in engineering for fault detection in rotating machinery components.<ref name="Parker2000">{{cite journal |last1=Parker |first1=B. E. |last2=Casada |first2=T. A. |last3=Forbes |first3=G. L. |title=Fault diagnostics using statistical change detection in the bispectral domain |journal=Mechanical Systems and Signal Processing |date=2000 |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=561–570 |doi=10.1006/mssp.2000.1299}}</ref>
Polyspectra have also become a tool in quantum physics for analysing records of quantum measurements.
<ref name = "norris2016">{{cite journal 
| last1 = Norris | first1 = Leigh M. 
| last2 = Paz-Silva | first2 = Gerardo A. 
| last3 = Viola | first3 = Lorenza 
| title = Qubit Noise Spectroscopy for Non-Gaussian Dephasing Environments 
| journal = Physical Review Letters 
| volume = 116 
| issue = 15 
| article-number = 150503 
| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.150503 
| url = https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.150503 
| arxiv = 1512.01575 
}}</ref>
The applications of quantum polyspectra range from quantum transport over single photon detection to spin noise measurements.
<ref name="emary2007">{{cite journal 
| last1 = Emary | first1 = C. 
| last2 = Marcos | first2 = D. 
| last3 = Aguado | first3 = R.

}}</ref>
